title: A Fed Official Just Said What Markets Were Dreading. India Has the Most to Lose.
excerpt: Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack warns the central bank may need to raise interest rates soon. For India, already bleeding foreign capital, a rate hike would accelerate the rupee's slide and force the RBI into an impossible choice.
body:
Cleveland Federal Reserve President Beth Hammack stood before the City Club of Cleveland on Tuesday and said the thing that central bankers usually take months to build toward: the Fed may need to raise interest rates soon.

"If we wait for definitive evidence that high inflation has become embedded in the economy, it may require larger policy adjustments, at greater cost," Hammack said in prepared remarks. "If recent trends continue, it may soon be appropriate to act."

Hammack is not just any Fed official. She holds a vote on the Federal Open Market Committee this year, making her words a direct signal of where rate-setting power may move. And she did not mince them: "I'm more concerned about the growing risks of persistently elevated inflation than the risks to full employment, and that monetary policy may not be sufficiently restrictive to bring inflation down to 2 percent."

## Why India Should Be Paying Close Attention

The Fed's benchmark rate currently sits at 3.5% to 3.75%. Markets had spent most of 2025 pricing in rate cuts. That expectation is now dead. Interest rate futures are pricing the next move as a hike — the first since 2023.

For India, the implications cascade quickly. The country has already lost its position as the world's sixth-largest stock market by capitalisation, dropping to seventh last week as South Korea's AI chip boom overtook it. Foreign portfolio investors have pulled billions from Indian equities over the past month, driven by the Iran war's impact on oil prices and the widening US-India interest rate differential.

A Fed rate hike would widen that differential further. Capital chases yield, and when the world's reserve currency offers higher returns, money flows out of emerging markets. The rupee, already under pressure from a $12 billion silver import bill and a ballooning oil deficit, would face fresh selling pressure.

## The RBI's Impossible Bind

The Reserve Bank of India is already caught between two fires. The Iran war has pushed Brent crude past $97, inflating India's import bill and stoking domestic price pressures. A weak monsoon forecast — potentially the driest in 11 years — threatens food prices. Together, they make a case for tighter monetary policy.

But the economy is also slowing. GDP growth, while still positive, has decelerated. Credit growth is softening. Small and medium businesses, which employ the bulk of India's workforce, are feeling the squeeze from elevated input costs. Raising rates to defend the rupee risks choking the real economy.

Governor Sanjay Malhotra faces his hardest rate decision at the RBI's upcoming review. Until Tuesday, the calculus was uncomfortable but manageable — hold rates, monitor inflation, hope the Iran situation resolves. Hammack's comments change the equation by adding a new variable: the possibility that the US will actively tighten, pulling capital away from India at exactly the moment it can least afford to lose it.

## The Broader Pattern

Hammack is not alone. Fed Governor Michelle Bowman, speaking in Reykjavik, was more cautious but acknowledged that if the Iran conflict proves prolonged, she would reconsider her risk assessment. The FOMC meets on June 16-17 under new Chair Kevin Warsh, who initially favored cuts but is now operating in an environment where that position has become untenable.

The practical outcome for Indian investors and businesses is straightforward: the era of easy global money is not coming back anytime soon. Companies that borrowed in dollars expecting rate cuts will face higher refinancing costs. IT firms that rallied 7% in two sessions on AI demand hopes may find that rally capped if the dollar strengthens further.

For the 4.5 million Indian Americans and NRIs who move money between rupee and dollar accounts, the calculus shifts too. A stronger dollar means remittances buy more rupees — good for families receiving money, painful for those sending it home to pay EMIs on Indian property loans.

The Fed hasn't raised rates yet. But the fact that a voting member is publicly building the case means the institution is preparing the ground. India's policymakers would be wise to prepare for that world rather than hope it doesn't arrive.
author: Diaspora Desk
